solution: The student picks exactly ONE course, and it may come from either list, so the two lists are mutually exclusive alternatives. By the addition principle the number of choices is \(5 + 3 = 8\). (The product \(5 \times 3 = 15\) would count the number of ways of taking one morning course AND one evening course, which is a different question.)
why: "Either ... or" with exclusive alternatives is the addition principle, not the multiplication principle.

solution: Here the student studies one morning course AND one evening course, so the two decisions are made in succession and independently. By the multiplication principle the number of choices is \(7 \times 3 = 21\). (Option D, \(7 + 3 = 10\), would be the count if only one course in total were chosen.)
why: "One in the morning and one in the evening" is a simultaneous pair, so multiply.

solution: Persons of the same nationality must sit together, so treat each nationality as a single block. There are three blocks (Indian, American, English), which can be ordered among themselves in \(3!\) ways. Within the blocks the members may be permuted freely: \(8!\) for the Indians, \(4!\) for the Americans and \(4!\) for the Englishmen. Total \(= 3!\,8!\,4!\,4!\), which is option B. Option D omits the \(3!\) that orders the blocks themselves.
why: The blocks must themselves be arranged, contributing the factor \(3!\) that option D drops.

solution: Total arrangements of \(10\) papers \(= 10!\). Count the arrangements in which the best and the worst DO come together by tying them into one block: \(9\) objects arrange in \(9!\) ways and the two tied papers can be ordered in \(2!\) ways, giving \(2 \times 9!\). Hence the required number is \(10! - 2 \times 9! = 10 \times 9! - 2 \times 9! = (10-2)\,9! = 8 \times 9!\).

With \(4\) boys and \(3\) girls the only alternating pattern possible is B G B G B G B, since a row of \(7\) alternating seats must begin and end with the larger group. The pattern is therefore forced (there is exactly one pattern, not two). The \(4\) boys fill the \(4\) boy-positions in \(4!\) ways and the \(3\) girls fill the \(3\) girl-positions in \(3!\) ways, so the total is \(4! \times 3! = 24 \times 6 = 144\). Option B, \(288\), is what one gets by wrongly doubling for a second (impossible) pattern beginning with a girl.
why: With counts \(4\) and \(3\) the alternating pattern is unique, so there is no factor of \(2\).

solution: A triangle is determined by any three of the polygon's vertices, and no three vertices of a convex polygon are collinear, so every choice gives a genuine triangle. The number of triangles is \({}^{8}C_{3} = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 56\).

The choices from the two parts are independent, so multiply. From part A: \({}^{10}C_{8} = {}^{10}C_{2} = \frac{10 \times 9}{2} = 45\). From part B: \({}^{10}C_{5} = \frac{10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6}{5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 252\). Total \(= 45 \times 252 = 11340\).

Exactly one person is to sit between the two brothers, so form a block of three seats: brother, that person, brother. The middle person can be chosen from the remaining \(8\) people in \(8\) ways. Now arrange this block together with the other \(7\) people around the round table: that is \(8\) objects in a circle, giving \((8-1)! = 7!\) arrangements. Finally the two brothers can be interchanged within the block in \(2!\) ways. Total \(= 8 \times 7! \times 2! = 8! \times 2! = 2! \times 8!\), since \(8 \times 7! = 8!\).
why: The \(8\) choices of the middle person absorb into \(7!\) to give \(8!\), so the answer is \(2!\,8!\) and not \(2!\,7!\).

solution: BANANA has \(6\) letters: A three times, N twice and B once. Total arrangements \(= \frac{6!}{3!\,2!} = \frac{720}{12} = 60\). Arrangements with the two N's together: tie them into one block, leaving the objects \(\{[\text{NN}], \text{A}, \text{A}, \text{A}, \text{B}\}\), i.e. \(5\) units with A repeated thrice, giving \(\frac{5!}{3!} = \frac{120}{6} = 20\) (the identical N's contribute no internal factor). Hence the number with the N's NOT adjacent is \(60 - 20 = 40\).
why: \(\frac{6!}{3!2!} - \frac{4!}{3!} = 60 - 4 = 40\); the identical N's give no \(2!\) inside the block.

solution: Total circular arrangements of \(7\) people \(= (7-1)! = 6! = 720\). Arrangements with the two females together: tie them into one block, giving \(6\) objects in a circle, \((6-1)! = 5! = 120\), and the two females can be interchanged in \(2!\) ways, so \(120 \times 2 = 240\). Required \(= 720 - 240 = 480\). Check by the gap method: seat the \(5\) males in a circle in \((5-1)! = 24\) ways, then place the two females in two of the \(5\) gaps in \({}^{5}P_{2} = 20\) ways, giving \(24 \times 20 = 480\).
why: \(6! - 2 \times 5! = 720 - 240 = 480\), confirmed independently by the gap method \(4! \times {}^{5}P_{2}\).
